catalog_quote: Stress in Karo is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. The following sections describe in turn: word stress, phrase stress, vocative stress and irregular stress. 2.1.1.1 WORD STRESS Word stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. ... /jəlma/ [jə́lma] person ... /pəkpək/ [pə́ʔpəʔ] hit ... /idaramina/ [idařamína] be sought by him. If the penultimate syllable is open and contains /ə/, stress usually shifts to the last syllable: /mədem/ [mədə́m] sleep, ... /pərləgo/ [pəřləgó] dry season. sweep_summary: Batak Karo (bata1293) had a single title-keyword hit, Kushnick 2013 (Human Nature 24:268-279), which the PubMed abstract shows to be an evolutionary-anthropology study of foot-size attractiveness (the keyword match is 'Feet'); it is irrelevant to word stress and silent on the catalog. The catalog's deciding source, Woollams 1996 §2.1.1 pp. 11-13, was re-read from the PDF and page image we hold and confirms the classification (penultimate stress, open-schwa penult shifts to final except before /ŋ, h/ or suffix -i/-en; non-phonemic), as does Neumann 1922 §8 pp. 9-10 (same core rule, differing only on doubled roots, which Woollams fn. 5 corrects). catalog's classification stands; no supersession.

new_statements.reading: Non-phonemic, right-edge penultimate word stress; a light (open, schwa) penult repels stress to the final syllable except before final /ŋ, h/ or suffix -i/-en — a full-vs-reduced-vowel weight system, exactly as the catalog codes it (classification weight). Neumann 1922 §8 states the same core rule in Dutch. This is the catalog's existing deciding source, re-read here; nothing newer or more authoritative was found.

audit.reasoning: The classification (penultimate stress; open schwa penult repels stress to the final unless the final begins with /ŋ, h/ or contains suffix -i/-en; right edge; full-vs-reduced-vowel weight) rests on the modern reference grammar (Woollams 1996, PL C-130), which we hold as PDF with page images; the deciding quotation is verbatim on p. 11-12 at the stated locator, including fn. 5. The older primary that StressTyp2 uses (Neumann 1922 §8, pp. 9-10) is also held and states the same core rule (penult; open penult with toneless e -> final), differing only on doubled roots, which Woollams explicitly corrects. The 2024 Kaufman & Himmelmann areal survey still draws its Karo Batak data from Woollams 1996:11-12, so no newer phonological or instrumental study appears to exist

sources.note: Penultimate word stress; an open schwa penult yields stress to the final unless the final begins with /ŋ, h/ or carries suffix -i/-en; phrase stress on the last word of a phrase; vocative stress on the final syllable; about ten irregular final-stressed words (§2.1.1.4). Fn. 5: contra Neumann 1922:10 and Adelaar 1981:2, doubled roots take regular penultimate stress. Fn. 6: rejects Tarigan & Tarigan 1979:84's claim of phonemic stress ([báyu] vs [bayú]) as vocative stress.

sources.quote: § 8. DE KLEMTOON. Als regel geldt dat [de voorlaatste lettergreep] van een woord den hoofdklemtoon heeft. [...] Uitzondering op dezen regel: heeft de voorlaatste lettergreep een toonlooze e, en is de lettergreep open, dan valt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep: medem „slapen, liggen" [...] Is evenwel de lettergreep gesloten, dan volgt men den gegeven regel [...] Woorden met herhaalden stam hebben een gelijkwaardigen klemtoon op elk deel, aldus: gakgak „opwaarts zien" pekpek „slaan". — Translation: 'As a rule the penultimate syllable of a word bears the main stress. [...] Exception: if the penultimate syllable has a toneless e and is open, stress falls on the last syllable: medem "sleep, lie" [...] If the syllable is closed, the rule holds [...] Words with a repeated stem have equal stress on each part: gakgak, pekpek.'

sources.note: Same core rule as Woollams (penult; open schwa penult -> final); differs on doubled roots (equal stress on both parts), which Woollams 1996 fn. 5 explicitly corrects.
